interactions.label: A 2-year-old with stridor and cyanosis after swallowing a coin, a man with facia

params.question: A 2-year-old with stridor and cyanosis after swallowing a coin, a man with facial trauma and gurgling respirations, and a 55-year-old with bilateral epistaxis arrive simultaneously in casualty. Which clinical finding identifies the highest-priority patient?

answers.text: Bilateral epistaxis in a hypertensive patient — indicates posterior bleeding with risk of airway flooding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epistaxis threatens the circulation, not the airway. This patient is urgent but ranks third under the ABCDE framework.

answers.text: Stridor with cyanosis — indicates failed oxygen delivery with imminent cardiac arrest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cyanosis signals that oxygen delivery has already failed; cardiac arrest can follow within minutes, making this the most time-critical emergency.

answers.text: Gurgling respirations — indicates complete upper airway obstruction requiring immediate cricothyroidotomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gurgling indicates a partially compromised airway, not complete obstruction. This patient is second priority — the airway is evolving but some air exchange persists.

answers.text: Hypertension with active bleeding — indicates impending circulatory shock as the most time-critical threat

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Active haemorrhage is a circulatory threat, addressed under 'C' in the ABCDE sequence — only after airway (A) and breathing (B) are secured in higher-priority patients.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the ABCDE framework: airway compromise with failed oxygenation (cyanosis) takes priority over evolving airway compromise (gurgling) and circulatory threats (haemorrhage).
Exactly right. In the ABCDE framework, cyanosis with stridor is the most immediately life-threatening finding because it signals active hypoxia with impending cardiac arrest.

interactions.label: A 4-year-old presents with a plastic bead visible in the right nostril. During r

params.question: A 4-year-old presents with a plastic bead visible in the right nostril. During removal with a hook, the bead moves deeper and is no longer visible. What is the correct next step?

answers.text: Switch to forceps and attempt retrieval by grasping the bead blindly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blind instrumentation risks pushing the bead into the nasopharynx, where it could be aspirated into the larynx — a far more dangerous situation.

answers.text: Stop the attempt and refer for removal under general anaesthesia with airway protection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. If you cannot clearly see the foreign body, you cannot safely pass an instrument behind it. Referral for removal under general anaesthesia with airway protection is the safe course.

answers.text: Ask the child to blow the nose forcefully to expel the bead

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Forceful nose-blowing is unreliable in a distressed young child and may push the bead posteriorly, risking aspiration into the larynx.

answers.text: Apply posterior nasal suction via the oropharynx to draw the bead backward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Drawing a nasal foreign body posteriorly violates the cardinal principle: always move the object outward toward the nostril, never deeper toward the airway.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the two linked rules: always draw a foreign body outward, and if it is no longer visible, stop and refer for removal under general anaesthesia with airway protection.
Well done. The rule is clear: if you cannot see it, you cannot safely retrieve it. Stop and refer for removal under general anaesthesia.

interactions.label: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media and a perforated tympanic membra

params.question: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media and a perforated tympanic membrane needs topical antibiotic ear drops. Which prescription is safe?

answers.text: Neomycin — aminoglycosides provide effective gram-negative coverage for middle ear infections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neomycin is an aminoglycoside. With a perforated tympanic membrane, drops pass through the middle ear and reach the cochlea via the round window, causing irreversible sensorineural hearing loss.

answers.text: Ciprofloxacin — quinolones are not ototoxic at topical concentrations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Quinolone drops such as ciprofloxacin are safe even with a perforated tympanic membrane because they are not ototoxic at topical concentrations.

answers.text: Gentamicin — its broad spectrum makes it the first choice for chronic ear infections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside and is contraindicated when the tympanic membrane is perforated. It damages cochlear hair cells when it reaches the round window membrane.

answers.text: Neomycin with dexamethasone — the corticosteroid component protects the cochlea from aminoglycoside toxicity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adding a corticosteroid does not prevent aminoglycoside ototoxicity. The aminoglycoside still passes through the perforation and damages the cochlea via the round window.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: a perforated tympanic membrane means drops reach the cochlea through the round window. Aminoglycosides (neomycin, gentamicin) are ototoxic at the cochlea; quinolones (ciprofloxacin) are not.
Exactly right. When the tympanic membrane is perforated, only non-ototoxic drops — such as quinolones — are safe, because anything instilled can reach the cochlea via the round window.

interactions.label: When consenting a patient for mastoidectomy, stating that 'the risk of facial ne

params.question: When consenting a patient for mastoidectomy, stating that 'the risk of facial nerve injury is less than one percent' is sufficient disclosure of that risk.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Stating frequency without consequence is the most dangerous consent error. The patient must hear both: 'less than one in one hundred' AND 'it can cause permanent weakness affecting eye closure and the corner of the mouth.'
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — it is not sufficient. Frequency alone does not allow the patient to make an informed decision. The consequence must be named: facial nerve injury can cause permanent weakness affecting eye closure and the corner of the mouth.

interactions.label: At an occupational health screening, a factory worker's audiogram shows a dip at

params.question: At an occupational health screening, a factory worker's audiogram shows a dip at 4 kHz with normal thresholds at other frequencies. His daily noise exposure is 88 dB. What is the most appropriate action?

answers.text: Reassure the worker — a single-frequency dip is a normal variant requiring no follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 4 kHz dip in the context of noise exposure is not a normal variant. It is the earliest audiometric sign of noise-induced hearing loss and a key marker for occupational compensation.

answers.text: Recommend hearing protection and schedule periodic audiometric follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 4 kHz notch is the earliest sign of noise-induced hearing loss. The worker needs hearing protection and periodic audiograms, which serve as both clinical monitoring and a medicolegal safeguard.

answers.text: Immediately remove the worker from the noisy environment and file a disability compensation claim

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Immediate removal and compensation filing are premature. The 4 kHz notch is an early warning sign, not established disability. Protection and follow-up are the appropriate first steps.

answers.text: Repeat the audiogram after one month of noise avoidance to check for recovery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Noise-induced hearing loss is irreversible — the 4 kHz notch will not recover with noise avoidance. The goal is to prevent further progression through protection and monitoring.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the 4 kHz notch is the earliest sign of noise-induced hearing loss and is irreversible. The correct response is hearing protection and periodic audiometric follow-up, not reassurance or removal.
Well done. The 4 kHz notch is the sentinel sign of noise-induced hearing loss. Protection and periodic audiometry prevent progression and provide medicolegal documentation.
